revisions.title: The philosopher’s readiness for death
revisions.body: One way to hear this turn is as a reply to Cebes’ contradiction: if the gods guard us, why would a philosopher welcome death? Socrates answers by making philosophy a discipline of loosening the soul’s attachment to bodily pleasures and concerns. Death matters here because it completes that separation; the philosopher’s readiness is therefore presented as the culmination of a way of living, not as a wish to escape by force.

revisions.title: Purification and the test of courage
revisions.body: I read this stretch as a test of what philosophical courage means. The point is not simply to welcome death, but to ask what desire or fear rules the person who appears calm. The contrast invites us to distinguish a life oriented toward the soul’s independence from a mere exchange of one pleasure or fear for another. That keeps “practice of dying” from becoming a slogan: what kind of freedom does this composure express?

revisions.title: Hope as a practiced release
revisions.body: One way to hear this passage is as a test of what “hope” means. Socrates does not offer a bare promise that death will solve everything; he ties hope to a practiced reorientation, away from letting pleasure and pain dictate what is real. The image of release therefore names a discipline, not an automatic escape.

revisions.title: Two images, one missing guarantee
revisions.body: I read the two images here as a pressure test rather than a verdict. Simmias’s harmony invites us to imagine the soul as dependent on the body’s organization; Cebes’s weaver allows a soul to outlast several bodies without making it indestructible. Together, they expose the gap between surviving longer than the body and being guaranteed to survive death.

revisions.title: When disappointment turns against argument
revisions.body: One way to hear this warning is as a lesson in intellectual self-correction. A failed or shifting argument need not make argument itself the enemy; the danger is our temptation to blame reasoning before examining how we trusted, tested, and handled it. The scene therefore redirects frustration into renewed inquiry.

revisions.title: When harmony cannot lead
revisions.body: One way to read this turn is as a test of what kind of thing the soul must be. The harmony image makes it passive, tuned by bodily parts; Socrates’ counterexample imagines soul as the voice that can oppose appetite. The pressure point is not merely whether the image is elegant, but whether it leaves room for resistance.

revisions.title: Participation and the exclusion of opposites
revisions.body: One way to read this unit is as a tightening of the explanatory method: participation supplies a stable answer to what makes something one or two, while the later examples test how opposites are excluded. Three is not itself the opposite of even, yet it cannot admit evenness while remaining three. The section prepares this logic; it does not yet apply it to the soul and life.

revisions.title: Immortality, hesitation, and ethical stakes
revisions.body: One way to hear this section is as a hinge, not as a settled map of the soul’s future. I hear Cebes accepting the conclusion, while Simmias’s hesitation keeps it from sounding unanimously settled. Socrates then shifts from what immortality may establish to how one should care for the soul, before offering a qualified picture of its postmortem journey.

revisions.title: A story, not a settled map
revisions.body: I would hear this passage as a speculative story rather than a demonstrated geography. On that reading, the elaborate upper earth changes the scale of the conversation: our familiar world becomes a limited viewpoint, and the myth invites us to imagine what lies beyond it. Its force is imaginative enlargement, not a demand that we mistake a consoling picture for established fact.
